title: Fishing
objective: After this level you can explain how fishing feeds the world.
summary: Fishing and fish farming made a record 195 million tonnes of aquatic animals in 2024. The wild catch has been flat since the 1980s; farms took the lead in 2022.

cards.headline: Farms now raise more seafood than all the world's fishing boats catch.
cards.body: For almost all of history, eating from the sea meant hunting wild animals. In 2022 that quietly changed. Follow the world's seafood from the net to the farm and see why.

cards.fact: In 2024, fishing and fish farming produced a record 195 million tonnes of aquatic animals.
cards.context: That's fish, plus shellfish like mussels and shrimp, according to the UN's Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO). Shared out, it's enough for about 21 kg per person on Earth, as measured in 2023. That's roughly a packed suitcase of seafood for each of us, every year.

cards.headline: Protein for billions
cards.body: For 3.1 billion people, fish and other aquatic foods supply at least a fifth of all the animal protein they eat, FAO reports. That's not a garnish or a treat; it's dinner, week in and week out. For them, the ocean is less a view than a pantry.

cards.headline: The wild catch hit a ceiling
cards.body: Here's the twist. Since the late 1980s, the world's wild catch has barely grown, staying between about 86 and 94 million tonnes a year. Most of it comes from the sea: 80 of the 92 million tonnes caught in 2024. More people, more appetite, roughly the same catch. The ocean can only hand over so much.

mascot.line: Keep this twist: the wild catch stalled, so the growth came from farms.

cards.headline: Down on the fish farm
cards.body: So the growth came from farming. Aquaculture means raising fish, shellfish and other water animals, and in 2022 it produced more of them than all capture fisheries for the first time. By 2024, farms made 103 million tonnes, about 53% of the total. It's the switch from hunting to farming, happening at sea.

title: Overfishing
objective: After this level you can explain overfishing and how fisheries recover.
summary: Overfishing collapsed Newfoundland's cod: a 1992 ban meant for two years lasted 32. About 62% of stocks are fished sustainably, and swordfish show recovery works.

cards.headline: In 1992, Canada closed its biggest cod fishery for two years. It took 32.
cards.body: The fish were northern cod off Newfoundland. How does a sea full of fish run short, and what does it take to bring the fish back?

cards.headline: Faster than they can breed
cards.body: Overfishing means catching fish faster than the population can replace itself. NOAA puts it more precisely: fishing above the rate that gives the biggest catch a stock can sustain. Newfoundland's cod were overfished for decades, until on July 2, 1992, Canada banned commercial cod fishing, costing about 19,000 jobs directly. The pause was expected to last two years. A cautious commercial fishery reopened only in 2024. A sea can be emptied far faster than it refills.

cards.fact: In 2023, about 62% of assessed marine fish stocks were fished within sustainable levels.
cards.context: So roughly three stocks in eight were overfished, FAO reports. Count by catch instead, though, and about 73% of landings came from sustainable stocks, because the biggest stocks tend to be the best managed. Most of the fish actually landed come from healthy stocks; a big minority of stocks are in trouble.

mascot.line: Fish turn out to be excellent at comebacks. They mostly need us to stop interrupting.

cards.headline: How swordfish came back
cards.body: By the late 1990s, the average swordfish caught in US waters weighed about 41 kg, down from about 113 kg in the 1960s. Under an international rebuilding plan from 1999, countries cut catches and closed grounds to protect young swordfish. In 2009 the North Atlantic stock was declared rebuilt, a year ahead of target. It's not a one-off: by 2023, NOAA counted 50 US fish stocks rebuilt since 2000.

title: Shipping
objective: After this level you can explain how most goods cross the ocean.
summary: Around 80% of international trade by volume goes by sea, made cheap by containers from 1956. Ships make about 2.9% of emissions, and a net-zero plan is contested.

cards.headline: Four in five tonnes of goods traded between countries travel by ship.
cards.body: Not by plane, not by truck: by sea. How did the ocean become the world's main freight road, and what does all that hauling cost the climate?

cards.headline: The world's freight road
cards.body: UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD) estimates that around 80% of the volume of international trade in goods is carried by sea. Remember Level 1: it's one connected ocean, so the same water road links coasts on every continent. Ships don't need a road built for them. The ocean already is one.

cards.headline: The box that changed everything
cards.body: In 1956, trucking entrepreneur Malcolm McLean sent his ship Ideal X from Newark to Houston carrying 58 metal containers. Instead of loading loose cargo piece by piece, dockworkers could lift whole boxes. Loading the old way cost more than $5.80 a ton; loading McLean's containers cost about 16 cents. A plain steel box made the ocean cheap to cross.

cards.headline: Ships and the climate
cards.body: All that hauling burns fuel. The International Maritime Organization (IMO), the UN's shipping agency, estimated that shipping made about 2.9% of human-caused greenhouse gas emissions in 2018. In 2023 its members set a goal of net-zero emissions from international shipping by or around 2050. Agreeing on the goal turned out to be the easy part.

cards.headline: A fight over the fuel bill
cards.body: In April 2025, IMO members approved a Net-Zero Framework: a fuel standard plus a price on emissions. The EU, Brazil and Pacific island nations backed it. The United States called it a global carbon tax and opposed it, as did Saudi Arabia. In October 2025, members voted 57 to 49 to delay adopting it by a year. The ocean's freight road is also a negotiating table.

title: Energy From the Sea
objective: After this level you can explain offshore wind and oil.
summary: Offshore wells gave nearly 30% of the world's crude oil in 2015. Offshore wind began at Vindeby in 1991; floating turbines reach deep water, and fishers worry about space.

cards.headline: In 1991, Denmark put 11 wind turbines in the sea.
cards.body: Vindeby was the world's first offshore wind farm. Today the sea yields both oil and wind power. Why go to all the trouble of building out on the waves?

cards.headline: Oil under the sea floor
cards.body: In 2015, offshore wells in more than 50 countries supplied nearly 30% of the world's crude oil, the US Energy Information Administration reports. Most comes from shallow water, which is cheaper and easier to drill. But companies keep drilling deeper, notably off Brazil and in the Gulf of Mexico. Nearly a third of the world's oil comes from under the sea.

cards.headline: Why wind goes to sea
cards.body: Winds at sea are strong and consistent, says the US Department of Energy,. And offshore wind farms can sit near crowded coastal cities that need the power. Vindeby's 11 turbines proved the idea in 1991. The sea offers what a wind turbine wants most: room and a steady breeze.

cards.headline: Turbines that float
cards.body: Most offshore turbines stand on foundations fixed to the sea floor, which works only in fairly shallow water. Yet about two-thirds of US offshore wind potential lies over water too deep for that. The answer: turbines mounted on floating platforms. If you can't reach the bottom, float.

cards.headline: Who shares the water?
cards.body: The sea is already a workplace. For fishers, especially trawl and dredge boats, the worry is being pushed off traditional grounds, NOAA Fisheries notes. It also notes that sea life may cluster around turbine foundations, a reef effect. Energy developers and fishers are still working out how to share the same patch of ocean.

title: Ocean Pollution
objective: After this level you can explain the main kinds of ocean pollution.
summary: About 80% of ocean pollution comes from land, mostly as runoff. Fertilizer feeds dead zones, 19 to 23 million tonnes of plastic leak in yearly, and spills add oil.

cards.headline: Most of what pollutes the sea never went near a boat.
cards.body: NOAA says about 80% of the pollution reaching the ocean comes from the land. A drip of engine oil, a sprinkle of fertilizer, a wrapper in a storm drain. Follow a few of those journeys to the sea.

cards.headline: Death by a thousand drips
cards.body: Much of it is runoff: rain washing pollution off many small sources, like cars, farms and septic tanks, into rivers and then the sea. Millions of engines each drop a little oil on roads every day, and much of it ends up in the ocean. No single drip looks like a disaster. Together, they make the land the ocean's biggest polluter.

mascot.line: Too much food, then too little oxygen. That twist is the whole story of a dead zone.

cards.headline: How fertilizer suffocates the sea
cards.body: Fertilizer feeds crops, and it feeds algae too. Every summer, nutrients from farms and cities across the Mississippi-Atchafalaya River Basin reach the Gulf of Mexico. Algae bloom, die and rot, and the rotting uses up the oxygen in the water. Fish swim away or die. That's a dead zone, and it can start on a farm far from any coast.

cards.headline: Plastic, and the occasional catastrophe
cards.body: UNEP estimates 19 to 23 million tonnes of plastic waste leak into lakes, rivers and seas every year. And sometimes pollution arrives all at once. In 2010 the Deepwater Horizon blowout killed 11 workers and spilled about 507 million liters of oil over 87 days, the largest marine oil spill in US history. Spills make the headlines; most of the mess arrives quietly, from land.

title: Protected Seas
objective: After this level you can explain marine protected areas.
summary: Countries control resources up to 200 nautical miles out; the high seas beyond gained a treaty in 2026. About 10% of the ocean is protected, and scientists debate reserves.

cards.headline: Nearly two-thirds of the ocean lies beyond any country's jurisdiction.
cards.body: So who looks after it? In January 2026, a new treaty gave the world a way. First, though: who controls which parts of the sea, and what does protecting a patch of it mean?

cards.headline: Lines on the water
cards.body: Remember Level 1: the ocean's borders are lines people drew. Here are some more. Under the 1982 UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, a coastal country controls the fish, oil and other natural resources in its exclusive economic zone, up to 200 nautical miles (about 370 km) out. Beyond lie the high seas, which cover nearly two-thirds of the ocean.

mascot.line: People mix these up: many protected areas still allow fishing. No-take reserves don't.

cards.headline: Protected, partly or fully
cards.body: A marine protected area (MPA) gives part of the sea extra protection. Many still allow some fishing; the strictest, no-take reserves, ban fishing and other extraction. As of April 2026, about 10% of the ocean lay in protected areas, IUCN reports. In 2022, countries agreed to protect 30% of land and sea by 2030.

cards.headline: A treaty for the high seas
cards.body: The High Seas Treaty, an agreement under the Law of the Sea convention, entered into force on January 17, 2026. It lets countries create protected areas on the high seas. There's plenty of room to fill: in April 2026, protected areas covered only about 1.66% of them.

cards.headline: Do reserves work? Two scientists disagree
cards.body: In 2018, marine ecologists Enric Sala and Sylvaine Giakoumi reviewed studies and found fish biomass in no-take reserves averaged 570% more than in unprotected waters (a corrected figure). Fisheries scientist Ray Hilborn replied that the estimate was too high, and that real protection of sea life will come from how we manage the waters that are fished. The argument is over which tool does the most good.

title: Pirates
objective: After this level you can describe real pirates and what their lives were like.
summary: Walking the plank is mostly myth. Golden-age pirates voted for captains, followed written codes and spent loot fast. Blackbeard's flagship lasted barely seven months; he died in 1718.

cards.headline: Walking the plank? Mostly a storybook invention.
cards.body: Pirates threw victims overboard or marooned them instead, says Royal Museums Greenwich. Real pirate life was stranger than the movies, and in some ways more orderly. Meet the real thing.

cards.headline: Blackbeard's short, loud career
cards.body: The so-called golden age of piracy lasted less than 50 years, and one of its most famous careers was brief. On November 28, 1717, Blackbeard's crew captured the French slave ship La Concorde and made it his flagship, Queen Anne's Revenge. In June 1718 it ran aground entering what is now Beaufort Inlet, North Carolina. That November 22, he was killed in battle at Ocracoke Inlet. The flagship lasted barely seven months.

cards.headline: Votes and written rules
cards.body: Pirate ships ran on paperwork. Many captains adopted codes of conduct to run the ship fairly, and crews often voted for their captain and could vote out a bad one. One code supposedly promised 800 pieces of eight to a man who lost a limb, with smaller sums for lesser injuries. Outlaws, yes, but outlaws with rules.

cards.headline: X doesn't mark the spot
cards.body: Pirates almost never buried treasure. They mainly spent it quickly, and they drew no treasure maps. Captain William Kidd was a rare exception: treasure he hid on Gardiners Island, off Long Island, in 1699 was dug up and used as evidence at his trial. For historians, the real treasure is on the sea floor: divers found the wreck of Queen Anne's Revenge in Beaufort Inlet in 1996, and archaeologists have studied it since.

title: Sea Monsters and Myths
objective: After this level you can explain the real animals behind sea-monster legends.
summary: Columbus's 1493 mermaids were likely manatees; sirenians are named for the Sirens. Sea serpents fit giant oarfish, and kraken tales grew from washed-up squid remains.

cards.headline: In 1493, Christopher Columbus reported three mermaids.
cards.body: On January 9, 1493, near today's Dominican Republic, he wrote that he had seen them, and that they were not as beautiful as they are painted. They were most likely manatees. Most sea monsters began like that: a real animal, seen badly.

cards.headline: Meet the mermaids
cards.body: Manatees and dugongs belong to a group of mammals called the sirenians, named after the Sirens of Greek myth. Britannica says they are believed to be the basis of the mermaid myth. So the legendary sea maiden was, most likely, a sea cow with good publicity.

cards.headline: The sea serpent
cards.body: The giant oarfish is the longest bony fish, documented at about 8 m, with a silver ribbon of a body. It lives about 200 to 1,000 m down, and one at the surface is usually in trouble and stranding itself. London's Natural History Museum puts it at the top of the list of real animals behind sea-serpent tales. A serpent that rarely surfaces, and only when dying, is a perfect rumor.

mascot.line: Notice the pattern: each monster here started as a real animal, seen badly.

cards.headline: Monsters on the map
cards.body: In 1539, Olaus Magnus published the Carta Marina, a large map of Scandinavia famous for the monsters swimming in its seas. Northern tales of the kraken were likely fed by real finds: rotted remains of giant squid and large octopuses washing up on beaches, which people tried to explain. Every monster on that map was a question nobody could yet answer.

title: Helping the Ocean
objective: After this level you can name practical ways people protect the ocean.
summary: Cleanups count what they collect, and the counts show which rules work. Catch limits and protected areas help. Plastics talks are split, and cutting CO2 matters too.

cards.headline: Volunteers picking up trash helped show a law was working.
cards.body: Protecting the ocean sounds enormous. In practice, it's often small, specific and measurable. Here are the tools people are using, and the argument over the next one.

cards.headline: A trash bag is also a data set
cards.body: Since 1986, over 19 million volunteers in Ocean Conservancy's International Coastal Cleanup have collected over 400 million pounds (about 181 million kg) of trash. They also record every item by type. That tally shows what to target, and whether rules work: after Washington, D.C., banned foam food containers in 2016, teams monitoring the Anacostia River saw less foam entering the water.

cards.headline: Tools that already work
cards.body: Some of the best tools are ones this chapter has met. Catch cuts and closed grounds rebuilt North Atlantic swordfish by 2009, and NOAA counts 50 US stocks rebuilt since 2000. Protected areas cover about 10% of the ocean, with a goal of 30% by 2030. Not glamorous. Just effective.

cards.headline: The plastics argument
cards.body: In August 2025, talks in Geneva on a global plastics treaty ended without agreement. The High Ambition Coalition of countries wants rules across plastic's whole life cycle, including how much is produced. The Like-Minded Countries, mostly oil producers, favor a treaty focused on waste and recycling. Governments planned to resume negotiating later in 2026.

cards.headline: The lever far from the beach
cards.body: In 2021 the IPCC concluded that human-caused carbon dioxide emissions are, virtually certainly, the main driver of the surface ocean's current acidification. So cutting emissions, from power plants to cargo ships, is ocean protection too, even when it happens nowhere near a coast.
